title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
Suppose the objective is an expectation under a distribution controlled by a parameter θ:
\[
J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim q_\theta(x)}\left[f(x)\right],
\qquad
\theta^\star
=
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta} J(\theta).
\]
The parameter θ appears in the sampling distribution q_θ. A sample drawn by an ordinary random number generator does not retain a differentiable path from x back to θ. We therefore need an estimator of the derivative of J(θ) with respect to θ.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
Suppose the objective is an expectation under a distribution controlled by a parameter θ:
\[
J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim q_\theta(x)}\left[f(x)\right],
\qquad
\theta^\star
=
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta} J(\theta).
\]
The parameter θ appears in the sampling distribution q_θ. A sample drawn by an ordinary random number generator does not retain a differentiable path from x back to θ. We therefore need an estimator of the derivative of J(θ) with respect to θ.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
2 The score function estimator
Differentiating the density inside the integral gives
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int f(x)\,\nabla_\theta q_\theta(x)\,dx.
\]
Using the identity below
\[
\nabla_\theta q_\theta(x)
=
q_\theta(x)\,\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(x),
\]
we obtain the score function gradient
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim q_\theta}
\left[
  f(x)\,\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(x)
\right].
\]
This identity is general. It requires a differentiable log density, but it does not require f to be differentiable.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
3 The pathwise estimator
Assume a sample from q_θ can be written as a differentiable transformation of parameter free noise:
\[
\varepsilon \sim p(\varepsilon),
\qquad
x = g_\theta(\varepsilon),
\]
where the distribution p does not depend on θ. The same objective becomes
\[
J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon \sim p(\varepsilon)}
\left[
  f\!\left(g_\theta(\varepsilon)\right)
\right].
\]
Now θ appears inside the deterministic transformation g_θ. Under the usual conditions for exchanging differentiation and expectation, the gradient is
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon \sim p(\varepsilon)}
\left[
  \nabla_\theta f\!\left(g_\theta(\varepsilon)\right)
\right].
\]
This is the pathwise gradient estimator, commonly called the reparameterization trick.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
4 A Gaussian example
Let the sampling distribution be a unit variance Gaussian with mean θ, and let the objective function be the square of the sample:
\[
q_\theta(x) = \mathcal{N}(\theta, 1),
\qquad
f(x) = x^2.
\]
The objective has a closed form:
\[
J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}\left[x^2\right]
=
\theta^2 + 1.
\]
Its exact gradient is
\[
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = 2\theta.
\]

4.1 Score function gradient
For the Gaussian mean,
\[
\nabla_\theta \log q_\theta(x) = x - \theta.
\]
One Monte Carlo sample therefore gives the estimator
\[
G_{\mathrm{score}}
=
x^2(x-\theta).
\]
Write the sample as x = θ + ε, with standard normal noise ε. The estimator has mean 2θ and variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(G_{\mathrm{score}}\right)
=
\theta^4 + 14\theta^2 + 15.
\]


4.2 Pathwise gradient
The reparameterized sample is
\[
x = \theta + \varepsilon,
\qquad
\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1).
\]
Differentiating the sampled objective with respect to θ gives
\[
G_{\mathrm{path}}
=
\nabla_\theta (\theta + \varepsilon)^2
=
2(\theta + \varepsilon).
\]
This estimator also has mean 2θ, while its variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(G_{\mathrm{path}}\right) = 4.
\]
For an average over n independent samples, both variances are divided by n:
\[
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\overline{G}_{\mathrm{score}}\right)
=
\frac{\theta^4 + 14\theta^2 + 15}{n},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\overline{G}_{\mathrm{path}}\right)
=
\frac{4}{n}.
\]
The pathwise estimator removes the fourth order growth in θ that appears in the score function estimator for this example.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
section: 5 What the change of variables accomplishes
text:
5 What the change of variables accomplishes
The reparameterization does not alter the distribution of x or the optimization objective. It moves the parameter from the distribution used for sampling into a differentiable deterministic map. Automatic differentiation can then follow the path from f(g_θ(ε)) back to θ while holding the sampled noise ε fixed.

title: Reparameterization Gradients
text:
6 References

Ronald J. Williams. Simple Statistical Gradient-Following Algorithms for Connectionist Reinforcement Learning. 1992.

title: Why the Residual Variance Estimator is Unbiased
text:
Under the usual notation,
\[Y = X\beta + \epsilon\]
where \(X\) is an \(n \times (p+1)\) matrix, that is, \(n\) rows of datapoints and \(p+1\) variables, and
\[\hat Y = X\hat\beta, \qquad \hat\beta = (X'X)^{-1}X'Y \implies \hat\beta' = Y'X(X'X)^{-1}.\]
Expanding the residual sum of squares,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2 & = (Y - \hat Y)'(Y - \hat Y) \\
& = \big(X(\beta - \hat \beta) + \epsilon\big)'\big(X(\beta - \hat \beta) + \epsilon\big)\\
& = \underbrace{(\beta - \hat \beta)'X'X(\beta - \hat \beta)}_{\text{term 1}} + \underbrace{\epsilon'X (\beta - \hat \beta)}_{\text{term 2}} + \underbrace{(\beta - \hat \beta)'X'\epsilon}_{\text{term 3}} + \epsilon'\epsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Simplifying the individual terms.
Term 1:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(\beta - \hat \beta)'X'X(\beta - \hat \beta) &= (\beta - (X'X)^{-1}X'Y)'X'X(\beta - (X'X)^{-1}X'Y)\\
&= (\beta' - Y'X(X'X)^{-1})X'X(\beta - (X'X)^{-1}X'Y) \\
&= \beta'X'X\beta - Y'X\beta - \beta'(X'X)(X'X)^{-1}X'Y + Y'X(X'X)^{-1}X'Y \\
&= \beta'X'X\beta - (\beta'X' + \epsilon')X\beta - \beta'(X'X)(X'X)^{-1}X'Y \\
&\quad + (\beta'X' + \epsilon')X(X'X)^{-1}X'Y \qquad (\text{substituting } Y') \\
&= - \epsilon'X\beta + \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'Y \qquad (\text{some terms cancel}) \\
&= - \epsilon'X\beta + \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'(X\beta + \epsilon) \qquad (\text{substituting } Y) \\
&= \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Term 2:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon'X (\beta - \hat \beta) &= \epsilon'X(\beta - (X'X)^{-1}X'Y)\\
&= \epsilon'X(\beta - (X'X)^{-1}X'(X\beta+\epsilon)) \qquad (\text{substituting } Y) \\
&= -\epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Term 3 is the same as term 2, namely \(-\epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon\). Collecting the terms,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2 &= \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon - \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon - \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon + \epsilon'\epsilon\\
&= \epsilon'\epsilon - \epsilon'X(X'X)^{-1}X'\epsilon\\
&= \epsilon'\epsilon - \epsilon'P\epsilon,
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(P\) is the projection matrix, which is symmetric and idempotent.
Now take the expectation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
E\big[\Sigma (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2\big] &= E(\epsilon'\epsilon - \epsilon'P\epsilon)\\
&= E(\epsilon'\epsilon) - E(\epsilon'P\epsilon)\\
&= n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2\,\mathrm{trace}(P)\\
&= (n-(p+1))\sigma^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
using the result below that \(\mathrm{trace}(P) = p+1\). Therefore
\[\frac{\Sigma (Y_i - \hat Y_i)^2}{\,n-(p+1)\,}\]
is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).

title: Why the Residual Variance Estimator is Unbiased
section: Proof that the trace of P equals p plus 1
text:
Proof that the trace of P equals p plus 1
The trace operator is commutative, \(\mathrm{trace}(AB)= \mathrm{trace}(BA)\). Therefore
\[\mathrm{trace}\big(\underbrace{X}_{A}\;\underbrace{(X'X)^{-1}X'}_{B}\big) = \mathrm{trace}\big((X'X)^{-1}X'X\big) = p+1.\]

title: Assumptions in Linear Regression
text:
A post explaining the popular assumptions involved in linear regression and their importance.
Most people usually think that the output of linear regression is only valid when the Linear, Independent, Normal, and Constant (LINC) assumptions are satisfied on the error terms. This is a post explaining what happens if those assumptions are violated.
Let me start by asking one basic question. Suppose we have our entire population of univariate datapoints \((X_1, Y)\). If one were to minimize squared error on this data and get the parameters \(b_0, b_1\) where
\[Y = b_0 + b_1 X_1 \quad \text{(1)}\]
but the error terms do not follow the assumptions above, what next?
You can safely use this model for predicting the relationship between \(X_1\) and \(Y\). There is no need to do any F-test or t-test. In fact, the LINC assumptions are needed only to perform the F-test or the t-test. The whole point of testing arises when we try to estimate the relationship \(b_1\) using the sample data available.
When we use the sample data and perform ordinary least squares, we get an estimate of \(b_1\) usually denoted \(\beta_1\). The first assumption in LINC, Linear, states that \(E(\epsilon)=0\), which means that \(\beta_1\) is an unbiased estimator of \(b_1\). Why?
\(Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \epsilon\) is the regression equation we get from the sample. If \(E(\epsilon)=0\), then \(\hat Y = b_0 + b_1 X_1\), which is exactly equation (1). This means that for a given value of \(X_1\) there could be multiple values of \(Y\), and our equation predicts the mean of these values, \(\hat Y\).
Having said that, the concept of \(r^2\) does not depend on these LINC assumptions. So we can still say what proportion of variation in the dependent variable, within the sample data, is explained by our regression equation.

title: Research
text: My research develops methods for language model inference, text classification, privacy, search, and statistical learning. I work on both mathematical questions and systems that are evaluated under production constraints.

title: Research
text:
Language model inference
I study how to reduce inference time while preserving model performance. My work covers autoregressive language models and diffusion language models.

Relaxed speculative decoding
Standard speculative decoding accepts a draft token only when a target model verifies it under an exact acceptance rule. Relaxed speculative decoding allows controlled disagreement between the draft and target models, increasing the number of accepted tokens while holding task performance fixed. The implementation was merged into HuggingFace transformers through the assistant_ensemble_weight generation argument.
Paper · Code · HuggingFace contribution


Fréchet profile decoding
Fréchet profile decoding accelerates diffusion language model inference. It generalizes factor based schedules and controls when token positions are updated during iterative generation.
Paper · Code · Project page


Conformal routing
CopRoute studies how to route language model requests while accounting for dependence in model outcomes. It uses conformal methods to control routing decisions without assuming independent errors.
Paper

title: Research
text:
Classification and privacy
I study when generative and discriminative text classifiers behave differently, how shortcuts and distribution shifts affect their predictions, and what privacy risks follow from modeling the input distribution.
This work includes an EMNLP 2025 Outstanding Paper on generative and discriminative text classification, studies of concept shift and ordinal labels, and membership inference attacks on generative classifiers and preference data.
Generative and discriminative classifiers · Privacy in generative classifiers · Privacy in preference data

My doctoral research studied dependence modeling with mixture models and copulas. The resulting work covers high dimensional clustering, model misspecification, reproducibility analysis, structural change in financial markets, and dependence in multi armed bandits.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
Let x₁, …, xₙ be independent observations from a model with density p(x | θ). Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter θ that makes the observed data most likely:
\[
\theta^\star
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} L(\theta),
\]
where the likelihood is
\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta).
\]
The parameter θ appears in every factor of this product. We differentiate the objective with respect to θ to find an optimizer. The product is mathematically valid, but it is inconvenient for both algebra and numerical computation.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
Let x₁, …, xₙ be independent observations from a model with density p(x | θ). Maximum likelihood estimation chooses the parameter θ that makes the observed data most likely:
\[
\theta^\star
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} L(\theta),
\]
where the likelihood is
\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta).
\]
The parameter θ appears in every factor of this product. We differentiate the objective with respect to θ to find an optimizer. The product is mathematically valid, but it is inconvenient for both algebra and numerical computation.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
2 The logarithm preserves the optimizer
The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on positive numbers. Therefore, the likelihood and log likelihood have the same maximizers:
\[
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} L(\theta)
=
\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\theta} \log L(\theta).
\]
The log likelihood is
\[
\ell(\theta)
=
\log L(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(x_i \mid \theta).
\]
Taking the logarithm changes the representation of the objective, but it does not change which value of θ maximizes it.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
3 Products become sums
Direct differentiation of the likelihood requires the product rule across all observations:
\[
\nabla_\theta L(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
  \nabla_\theta p(x_i \mid \theta)
  \prod_{j \ne i} p(x_j \mid \theta)
\right].
\]
The gradient of the log likelihood is additive:
\[
\nabla_\theta \ell(\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\nabla_\theta \log p(x_i \mid \theta).
\]
Each observation contributes one term. This form supports minibatch optimization because a batch can estimate the sum over the full data set.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
4 Log probabilities avoid numerical underflow
Individual densities or probabilities often lie between zero and one. Multiplying many such terms can produce a number smaller than the floating point system can represent. The computed likelihood then becomes zero even when every factor is positive.
The log likelihood replaces multiplication with addition. Small probabilities become finite negative log probabilities:
\[
\log\!\left(
  \prod_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i \mid \theta)
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(x_i \mid \theta).
\]
This representation preserves information that would be lost if the product underflowed to zero.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
5 Gaussian regression as an example
Assume a regression model with prediction μᵢ(θ) and independent Gaussian errors of variance σ²:
\[
x_i \mid \theta
\sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_i(\theta), \sigma^2\right).
\]
The log likelihood is
\[
\ell(\theta)
=
-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(x_i - \mu_i(\theta)\right)^2.
\]
When σ² is fixed, maximizing this expression with respect to θ is equivalent to minimizing the sum of squared errors:
\[
\theta^\star
=
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\theta}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left(x_i - \mu_i(\theta)\right)^2.
\]
The familiar squared error objective therefore follows from a Gaussian observation model.

title: Why Optimize Log Likelihood?
text:
6 Summary
Log likelihood is used because it preserves the maximum likelihood estimate, turns products into additive terms, simplifies differentiation, supports minibatch estimates, and avoids floating point underflow. These properties follow from the logarithm and the independence factorization. They do not require a different statistical model.

title: Convergence of Policy Iteration
text: First let’s see why the policy iteration algorithm works. It has two steps.

title: Convergence of Policy Iteration
text:
Policy evaluation step
\(v_n = r_{d_n} + \gamma P_{d_n}v_n\) is the general vectorial form of the system of linear equations.
Here, the terms \(r_{d_n}, P_{d_n}\) are the immediate rewards and the corresponding rows of the transition matrix. These terms depend on the policy \(\Pi_n\). Solving the above system of equations gives the values \(v_n\).

title: Convergence of Policy Iteration
Convergence of Policy Iteration
text:
Proof
From equation 2, we have
\[[I - \gamma P_{d_{n+1}}]v_{n+1} = r_{d_{n+1}}\]
From equations 1 and 2, we have
\[v_{n+1} \ge v_n\]
So the values increase monotonically with each iteration. This is the key to understanding why policy iteration does not get stuck at a local maximum.
A policy is a mapping over the state-action space. At every policy iteration step we look for at least one state-action pair that differs between \(\Pi_{n+1}\) and \(\Pi_n\) and check whether \(r_{d_{n+1}} + \gamma P_{d_{n+1}}v_n \ge r_{d_n} + \gamma P_{d_n}v_n\). Only if the condition holds do we solve the new system of linear equations.
Assume \(\Pi^{*}\) and \(\Pi^{\#}\) are the global and local optimum respectively, so that \(v_{*} \ge v_{\#}\). Suppose the algorithm is stuck at the local optimum. Then the policy improvement step will not stop at the local optimum state-action space \(\Pi^{\#}\), because there exists at least one state-action pair in \(\Pi^{*}\) that differs from \(\Pi^{\#}\) and yields a higher value of \(v_{*}\) compared to \(v_{\#}\). In other words, assuming \([I-\gamma P_{d_*}]\) is positive,
\[
\begin{aligned}
[I-\gamma P_{d_*}]v_* & \ge [I-\gamma P_{d_*}]v_{\#} \\
\implies r_{d_*} & \ge [I-\gamma P_{d_*}]v_{\#} \\
\implies r_{d_*} + \gamma P_{d_*}v_{\#} & \ge v_{\#} \\
\implies r_{d_*} + \gamma P_{d_*}v_{\#} & \ge r_{d_\#} + \gamma P_{d_\#}v_\#
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence policy iteration does not stop at a local optimum.
